# Encoding and Features {#sec-encoding}

Models take numbers. Categories, words and the bends in a numeric relationship have to become
numbers first, and the choice of encoding decides which functions of them are easy to learn. An
encoding can assert an order the data does not have, merge categories that should stay apart,
or, in one popular case, copy the label into the features. This chapter treats the common
encodings as choices on the representation lever, and measures the one that leaks.

## The problem

Given a categorical column, a numeric column whose effect is curved, or a column of text, which
representation lets the model learn the right function, and what does each representation
assume? For one encoding, target encoding, there is a second question. It is computed from the
labels, so how should it be fit without leaking them?

## Assumptions

1. **The model is fixed; only the representation changes.** Each demonstration holds the model
   constant (an unpenalized logistic regression or a linear regression) and changes only the
   encoding, so differences come from the representation.
2. **Levels and vocabularies are learned from training data only.** A level or a word first
   seen at test time has no column, unless the encoder reserves one or hashes it.
3. **For target encoding, rows are exchangeable.** With rows ordered in time, the encoding must
   also respect time ([Data Types and Their Structure](03-data-types.qmd#sec-data-types)).

## Derivation or demonstration

**One-hot and ordinal codes.** A one-hot encoding gives each level its own indicator column; an
ordinal encoding gives each level an integer. A linear model on one-hot columns can assign
every level its own effect. On an ordinal code it can fit only a straight line in the code,
asserting both an order and an equal spacing. In the demonstration, a category has six levels
whose effects (0, 3, −2, 1, −3, 2) are unrelated to their codes. Linear regression on the
one-hot encoding reached a test $R^2$ of 0.947, equal to the ceiling the noise allows. On the
ordinal code it reached 0.008
(`tests/test_encoding.py::test_ordinal_codes_impose_an_order_one_hot_does_not`).

{{< include ../includes/cards/one-hot-ordinal.md >}}

**Hashing.** With very many levels, or an open-ended set (identifiers, words), feature hashing
maps each level to one of $m$ columns by a hash function, with no stored vocabulary
[@weinberger2009feature]. Distinct levels that land in the same column share it. For a uniform
hash, $k$ levels occupy on average $m\,(1 - (1 - 1/m)^k)$ of the $m$ columns. Hashing 2,000
levels with scikit-learn's `FeatureHasher` used 880 of 1,024 columns (expected 879) and 1,775
of 8,192 (expected 1,775). Even with four times as many columns as levels, the 2,000 levels
fell into only 1,775 columns, so at least 225 of them share a column with another
(`tests/test_encoding.py::test_feature_hashing_collides_at_the_expected_rate`).

{{< include ../includes/cards/feature-hashing.md >}}

**Target encoding.** A high-cardinality category can instead be replaced by one number per
level: the mean target among training rows with that level, shrunk toward the global mean for
rare levels. scikit-learn's `TargetEncoder` follows Micci-Barreca's scheme of mixing the global
mean with the level's mean [@miccibarreca2001preprocessing]. The encoding is computed from the
labels, which makes it a supervised step, and
[Cleaning](04-cleaning.qmd#sec-cleaning) showed that supervised steps fit on the evaluation
rows fabricate signal. Here the evaluation rows are the training rows themselves. If each row's
encoding includes its own label, the feature carries that label into the model.

The demonstration adds one pure-noise feature to T1's classification task: a category with
1,000 levels, assigned at random. Over 20 seeds, with 2,000 training rows:

- **without the feature,** training and test accuracy were 0.746 and 0.752;
- **encoded on the same rows it was fit on,** training accuracy rose to 0.854 and test accuracy
  fell to 0.618. The model put a large coefficient (7.8, on a probability-scale feature) on
  noise;
- **cross-fitted,** where each row is encoded by an encoder fit on the other folds, as
  `TargetEncoder.fit_transform` does (here with a seeded 5-fold splitter), the result was 0.747
  and 0.751, with a coefficient of $-0.05$
  (`tests/test_leakage.py::test_target_encoding_without_cross_fitting_leaks`).

::: {.callout-note title="Result: an encoding fit on the labels must not see the row it encodes"}
A target encoding computed on the same rows it encodes includes each row's own label. With
many rare levels that is enough to turn pure noise into the strongest feature in training, and
the model is then worse on new data than without it. Cross-fitting, encoding each row with
statistics from the other folds, removes the leak.
:::

{{< include ../includes/cards/target-encoding.md >}}

**Splines and bins.** A numeric feature whose effect is curved defeats a linear model on the
raw value. Two encodings give the linear model a curve to fit. Discretization replaces $x$ by
indicators of intervals, and splines replace it by a basis of piecewise polynomials. On
$y = \sin(2x)$ plus noise, a linear regression on raw $x$ reached a test $R^2$ of 0.14. On 20
quantile bins it reached 0.82, and on a cubic spline basis with 8 knots 0.85, against a noise
ceiling of 0.85
(`tests/test_encoding.py::test_splines_and_bins_let_a_linear_model_fit_a_curve`).

{{< include ../includes/cards/splines-bins.md >}}

**Text: from counts to TF-IDF.** The simplest representation of a document counts its words,
discarding order. TF-IDF reweights the counts so that words common to every document count
less. In scikit-learn's default it multiplies the count $\text{tf}(t, d)$ of term $t$ in
document $d$ by $\ln\big((1 + n)/(1 + \text{df}(t))\big) + 1$, where $n$ is the number of
documents and $\text{df}(t)$ the number containing $t$, then scales each document's vector to
unit length (scikit-learn 1.9, `TfidfTransformer` docstring; a test reproduces its output from
this formula to 12 digits:
`tests/test_encoding.py::test_tfidf_matches_the_documented_formula`). Learned embeddings
replace this with vectors trained on other text, which belongs to the architecture books.

{{< include ../includes/cards/tf-idf.md >}}

**Images and audio.** Pixel intensities and audio samples are already numbers. Their encoding
questions are the representation and scale questions of the previous chapters: rescaling
intensities is affine ([Affine Scaling](05-affine-scaling.qmd#sec-affine)), and a spectrogram
is a change of representation
([Data Types and Their Structure](03-data-types.qmd#sec-data-types)).

::: {.callout-note title="In practice"}
In scikit-learn 1.9, `TargetEncoder().fit_transform(X, y)` cross-fits (`cv=5`), but
`fit(X, y).transform(X)` does not; its documentation notes that the second "does not equal" the
first. Use `fit_transform` on training data and `transform` on new data, or put the encoder in a
`Pipeline`. Its folds are shuffled without a fixed seed by default, so pass a splitter such as
`cv=KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)` for reproducible results (the `shuffle` and
`random_state` arguments are deprecated in 1.9). `TfidfVectorizer`'s default `token_pattern`
is `(?u)\b\w\w+\b`: tokens of two or more word characters (Unicode letters, digits or the underscore), so one-character words are dropped.
:::

## What it does to the learned model

An encoding sets the hypothesis space a fixed model can reach. One-hot columns let a linear
model fit any per-level effect; an ordinal code limits it to a line in an arbitrary order.
Splines let it fit smooth curves. Hashing lets colliding levels share an effect. Target encoding
compresses a category into one number, which is efficient when the number is honest and
destructive when it contains the label. In the last case the model learns to read the leak, and
on new data, where there is none, it is worse than if the feature had been left out.

## Failure modes

![Panel A: training (circles) and test (squares) accuracy of the same logistic regression with a pure-noise 1,000-level category left out, target-encoded on the rows it encodes, and cross-fitted (lines join each of 20 seeds). Panel B: the same linear regression fit to $y = \sin(2x)$ plus noise on raw $x$, on 20 quantile bins and on a cubic spline basis. Target encoding without cross-fitting turns noise into a training signal that fails on new data; bins and splines let a linear model fit a curve.](../images/encoding.png){#fig-encoding}

@fig-encoding shows the two central demonstrations. Further failures:

- **Unseen levels.** A level absent from training has no one-hot column and no target mean.
  scikit-learn's encoders raise an error or map it to a default (the global mean, for
  `TargetEncoder`); either way the model learns nothing about it.
- **Too many bins or knots.** Each bin or knot adds a parameter fit on fewer rows, so variance
  rises. Neither bins nor splines extrapolate beyond the training range.
- **Leakage across time.** A cross-fitted target encoding still averages labels from the
  future when rows are ordered in time, the same failure as a shuffled split.

## What the toy cannot show

The noise category is pure noise, and the curve is a single smooth function of one feature.
Real categories carry some signal and some noise in unknown proportions, and real text needs
far more than counts. The demonstrations show what each encoding can represent and how target
encoding leaks, not which encoding is best for a given dataset.
